title: Ines and the Undertow
premise: After his mother's funeral, Bram Okonkwo returns to the shuttered coastal house where she spent her final years, cataloging her silence: unlabeled tapes, unsent letters, a locked room. When a radio plays a song he knows she wrote and never recorded, credited to another woman, Bram begins tracing how his mother's music, name, and truth were taken by the person she loved most. His investigation forces him to confront his own twenty-year habit of almost speaking — about his father, his exile from the family, his complicity in her quiet. The novel ends at the water's edge, where Bram finally says goodbye aloud, records his mother's last song himself, and chooses truth over the loyalty that kept them both silent.
about_author: Elodie Sterling is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging the unpublished papers of deceased musicians before turning to fiction. She writes from a rented cottage on the Atlantic coast, where she claims the tide sets her revision schedule.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Silence
chapters.summary: Bram, POV, sorts through his mother Adaeze's belongings three days after the funeral: labeled boxes, blank cassettes, a room kept locked even in death. He catalogs objects instead of grieving, a habit twenty years old. Emotional beat: controlled grief cracking at the edges as he realizes he never knew what she withheld.

chapters.title: A Song Out of the Water
chapters.summary: Driving home, Bram hears a radio song whose melody he knows by heart — Adaeze hummed it all his childhood — credited to 'Marisol Vane.' He pulls over, shaking. POV Bram. Emotional beat: the vertigo of discovering a private inheritance was stolen and made public.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Knew
chapters.summary: Bram interviews the elderly neighbor Mrs. Calloway, who reveals Adaeze once played music openly, before 'the man from the label' started visiting. POV Bram with flashback texture. Emotional beat: first glimpse that his mother's silence was chosen under pressure, not natural.

chapters.title: The Locked Room
chapters.summary: Bram breaks into the locked room and finds a guitar, demo tapes dated 1989–1994, and letters addressed to Marisol Vane — unopened, returned. POV Bram. Emotional beat: awe curdling into anger; the evidence is physical now.

chapters.title: Marisol
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Marisol Vane, famous and dying of heart failure, watching a tribute documentary about herself and flinching at a melody she didn't write. Her manager dismisses her unease. Emotional beat: guilt as a physical illness; the thief is also a prisoner.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Bram's POV: 2003, the fight with his father over Adaeze's 'hobby,' the ultimatum, Bram's departure, the phone calls he let ring out. Emotional beat: Bram recognizes he abandoned his mother to protect his own peace — loyalty to the wrong parent.

chapters.title: Tape Side B
chapters.summary: Bram plays a demo tape; Adaeze's voice introduces each song with dates and one recurring phrase: 'for M., if she ever tells it.' POV Bram. Emotional beat: intimacy with the dead mother he never truly knew, and dread about what 'it' is.

chapters.title: The Label Man
chapters.summary: Bram tracks down Desmond Achebe, retired A&R executive, who admits Marisol's debut was built on demos submitted by an unnamed collaborator — and that contracts were signed in a hospital waiting room. POV Bram. Emotional beat: the machinery of theft revealed as banal paperwork.

chapters.title: Power Sits Where It Lands
chapters.summary: Desmond defends himself: 'She signed. Nobody holds a gun.' Bram sees how power corrupts through plausible deniability — including his own father's role as witness. POV Bram. Emotional beat: moral nausea; everyone chose comfort over truth.

chapters.title: Letters Returned Unopened
chapters.summary: Bram reads Adaeze's returned letters: not accusations but invitations — come hear me play, come say it to my face. Marisol never came. POV Bram. Emotional beat: grief reframed; his mother waited twenty years for a conversation that never happened.

chapters.title: The Daughter of the Thief
chapters.summary: POV Nia Vane, Marisol's daughter and heir apparent, who has always suspected the origin story was too clean. She finds her mother's hidden notebook of borrowed melodies. Emotional beat: inherited complicity; Nia must decide whether legacy or truth matters more.

chapters.title: Convergence at the Archive
chapters.summary: Nia contacts Bram after finding his name in the notebook margins. They meet in a university music archive, comparing evidence, wary allies. Alternating POV. Emotional beat: two children of silence recognizing each other across the theft.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Bram's brother Chidi arrives, furious: exposing this will shame their father's memory and the family name. POV Bram. Emotional beat: the central theme sharpened — Chidi offers loyalty without truth; Bram must refuse or repeat history.

chapters.title: Marisol Calls
chapters.summary: Marisol, against advice, phones Bram directly. She neither apologizes nor denies; she asks what Adaeze wanted. Bram answers: 'To be heard.' POV Marisol then Bram. Emotional beat: the confrontation both feared becomes strangely gentle.

chapters.title: The Hospital Waiting Room, Again
chapters.summary: Full flashback, dual timeline: 1994, Adaeze signing away rights while her husband watched and said nothing; Bram, age nine, outside the door. POV Adaeze. Emotional beat: the mother finally gets her own voice on the page — the novel's structural hinge.

chapters.title: Nia's Choice
chapters.summary: Nia publicly announces she will delay her debut album until authorship is resolved, detonating her career trajectory. POV Nia. Emotional beat: breaking generational complicity; power refused is power transformed.

chapters.title: Chidi Walks Out
chapters.summary: The brothers' final rupture: Chidi threatens legal obstruction and leaves. Bram stands alone with the tapes and understands saying goodbye means doing it unaccompanied. POV Bram. Emotional beat: loneliness accepted as the price of truth.

chapters.title: Credit Where Due
chapters.summary: The retraction goes public: streaming platforms relabel the songs, press descends, Desmond issues a lawyerly non-apology. Bram refuses interviews, keeping the focus on Adaeze's name. POV Bram. Emotional beat: vindication that feels hollow until he remembers it was never about him.

chapters.title: The Last Tape
chapters.summary: Bram finds a final cassette taped inside the piano bench: Adaeze's voice, weeks before death, singing an unfinished song and leaving the second verse 'for whoever comes looking.' POV Bram. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness; she trusted someone would come.

chapters.title: Marisol at the Door
chapters.summary: Marisol, frail, travels to the coastal house unannounced. She and Bram sit with the tapes; she weeps at Adaeze's spoken introductions. No absolution is asked or given. POV alternating. Emotional beat: reckoning without forgiveness — honesty as the only honest tribute.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Climax: at low tide, Bram records the unfinished song, completing the second verse in his mother's style, and speaks her name, her story, and his own apology into the recorder — out loud, properly, at last. POV Bram. Emotional beat: catharsis; the almost-said becomes said.

chapters.title: Undertow, Slack Tide
chapters.summary: Resolution: months later, the completed song releases under Adaeze Okonkwo's name; Nia produces, Marisol funds it anonymously. Bram visits the grave, tells Chidi the door stays open, and walks the shoreline as the tide turns. POV Bram. Emotional beat: quiet peace — truth survived, identity reclaimed, goodbye finished.
